content.title: How can Christians defend the Trinity to a Muslim neighbour?
content.summary: Confess one God clearly and explain the real disagreement.

answer.text: Begin with the Christian confession: one God in three distinct persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Christianity rejects three gods. Islam's affirmation of God's oneness does not remove its disagreement with this confession: Qur'an 112 denies begetting, and 4:171 rejects the language of three.

reasoning.text: The unity of God is explicit in Scripture.
The Son is distinguished from the Father while sharing divine identity.
The baptismal command names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together.

conclusion.text: The dispute is about the identity of the one God, not whether Christianity should permit three separate deities.

sections.text: Being and person answer different questions. The confession is not one person who switches roles, nor three beings who cooperate. Everyday objects cannot reproduce God's triune life; a simple illustration can mislead if it removes the distinction.
sections.title: Define before illustrating

sections.text: The Nicene confession calls the Son begotten, not made. This expresses his eternal relation to the Father, not a physical birth within the divine nature. The Word already is before creation and later takes flesh.
sections.title: Eternal, not physical, generation

content.objection: Does calling Jesus God divide God's oneness?

reply.text: The confession distinguishes persons without dividing the divine being. That answers a three-gods caricature; the positive reason for the doctrine is God's revelation in Scripture.

limit.text: Explaining what Christianity teaches does not make the disagreement disappear. We should acknowledge the Qur'anic rejection rather than claim the texts secretly teach the same doctrine.

prompt.text: Could I explain what we mean by one being and three persons, then hear which part you find difficult?
